tagline: The story of Israel and Judah from Elijah's departure to the fall of Samaria and of Jerusalem, told as the long working out of God's word through prophets and kings.
overview:
Second Kings picks up where 1 Kings stops, with Ahab dead and his son Ahaziah on Israel's throne. Its first half belongs largely to the prophet Elisha, who receives Elijah's mantle when Elijah is taken up in a whirlwind and then works a long series of wonders: purifying a spring, multiplying a widow's oil, raising a Shunammite woman's son, healing the Aramean general Naaman of skin disease, and blinding an Aramean raiding party. Around those stories the politics of the ninth century BC grind on. Moab rebels, Aram besieges Samaria, and then Jehu, anointed at Elisha's command, wipes out the house of Ahab and Jezebel in a bloody coup. In Judah, Ahab's daughter Athaliah seizes power and nearly destroys the line of David, until the priest Jehoiada crowns the hidden boy Joash.

The second half moves faster and darker. Assyria rises in the east and swallows the northern kingdom, and Samaria falls in 722 BC; chapter 17 pauses to explain why, in one of the Bible's longest theological reflections on history. Judah survives for another century and a quarter under a mix of kings. Hezekiah trusts the LORD when the Assyrian king Sennacherib surrounds Jerusalem, and the city is spared. His son Manasseh then leads Judah into the worst idolatry in its history. Josiah finds the Book of the Law in the temple and carries out the most thorough reform any king attempted, but it cannot turn back the judgment. Babylon replaces Assyria, Jerusalem is captured in 597 BC and destroyed in 587 or 586 BC, and the temple burns.

The book ends in exile with a quiet scene: King Jehoiachin, David's descendant, released from a Babylonian prison and given a seat at the king's table. Second Kings matters because it tells, without flinching, how the people of God lost everything they had been given, and it insists that this happened neither by accident nor because other gods were stronger. It also refuses to end in despair. The word of the LORD has proved true in judgment, and the promise to David is still alive.
author:
Like 1 Kings, the book is anonymous, and 1 and 2 Kings were originally a single work. A Jewish tradition preserved in the Babylonian Talmud names the prophet Jeremiah as the author of Kings. The link is real in one respect: 2 Kings 24:18-25:30 appears almost word for word as Jeremiah 52, and the two books share much of their language and outlook. Most scholars today think of an editor or school of editors who shaped older sources into the present book. Those sources are named in the text: the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel and the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, cited at the end of reign after reign, probably royal annals or works drawn from them. The long Elijah and Elisha narratives likely came from circles of prophets who kept those stories.

Since Martin Noth's work in the 1940s, many scholars have read Deuteronomy through 2 Kings as one Deuteronomistic History, judged by the standards of Deuteronomy: worship of the LORD alone, at the one place he chose. A common view (associated with Frank Moore Cross) sees a first edition in the reign of Josiah, whose reform is the book's high point, and a second edition during the exile that added the fall of Judah. Others argue for one exilic author working with sources. Conservative scholars generally accept the use of sources and editorial shaping while stressing the antiquity and reliability of the material.
date: The book in its final form cannot be earlier than about 561 BC, the year in which the Babylonian king Evil-merodach (Amel-Marduk in Babylonian records) released Jehoiachin from prison, the event told in the last paragraph (2 Kings 25:27-30). It says nothing of Cyrus's decree of 539/538 BC or of any return from exile, so most scholars place its completion in the middle of the sixth century BC, during the exile. Those who hold to an earlier edition under Josiah date it to the late seventh century BC, with the last chapters added later. The events the book covers run from about 852 BC, the death of Ahaziah of Israel, to 561 BC, a span of roughly three centuries. The chronology of the kings is complicated by co-regencies and by different ways of counting the first year of a reign, and scholars have proposed several reconstructions; dates for individual reigns in these notes are therefore approximate.
setting:
Second Kings is the story of a small people caught between empires. In the ninth century BC, Israel's main rival was Aram, the kingdom of Damascus, under kings such as Ben-hadad and Hazael. Assyria, centered on the Tigris in northern Mesopotamia, was already pressing west: Shalmaneser III fought a coalition that included Ahab at Qarqar in 853 BC, and his Black Obelisk shows Jehu, or his envoy, bowing and bringing tribute. From the reign of Tiglath-pileser III (745 to 727 BC), called Pul in 2 Kings 15:19, Assyria turned raiding into conquest, deporting populations and reducing kingdoms to provinces. Samaria fell in 722 BC after a siege begun by Shalmaneser V; his successor Sargon II claimed the capture and the deportation of its people. In 701 BC Sennacherib invaded Judah and besieged Lachish, a campaign known both from his own annals and from the reliefs of Lachish's fall that decorated his palace at Nineveh.

Assyria collapsed at the end of the seventh century. Nineveh fell in 612 BC, Josiah died at Megiddo in 609 BC when he confronted Pharaoh Neco of Egypt, and Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC. The Babylonian Chronicle records Nebuchadnezzar's capture of Jerusalem in 597 BC, and ration tablets from Babylon mention Jehoiachin, king of Judah, receiving provisions in exile. Several discoveries touch the book's world directly: the Mesha Stele, Moab's own account of throwing off Israel's rule (compare 2 Kings 3); the Tel Dan Stele, an Aramaic inscription that refers to the house of David; and the Siloam tunnel inscription, cut into the water tunnel usually connected with Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:20). The first readers were Judeans in Babylon or in the ruins of Judah, asking what their history meant.
purpose: Second Kings was written to explain the catastrophe of exile and to call its readers back to God. Its answer to the question of why the kingdoms fell is stated most fully in 2 Kings 17: Israel and Judah worshiped other gods, ignored the covenant, and refused the prophets the LORD sent to warn them. The fall was judgment, not the defeat of the LORD by the gods of Assyria or Babylon. The book also teaches its readers how to live in the ruins. It shows that repentance matters, even late (Hezekiah and Josiah are honored for it), and that God is patient far longer than anyone deserves. Finally, it keeps hope open. The release of Jehoiachin in the last verses is small, but it tells exiles that David's line has not been extinguished and that the story is not over.
story: Second Kings completes the history that begins in Joshua and runs through Judges, Samuel, and 1 Kings: the people brought into the land lose it. It follows directly from 1 Kings 22, where Ahab dies at Ramoth-gilead as Micaiah foretold. The prophets whose books stand later in the Bible preached during these same reigns: Amos and Hosea to the northern kingdom in the eighth century, Isaiah and Micah in Judah under Hezekiah and his predecessors, and Jeremiah, Zephaniah, and Habakkuk in Judah's last decades. First and 2 Chronicles retell the same period from Judah's side for the community after the exile, and Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai, and Zechariah tell of the return that 2 Kings does not reach. Lamentations mourns the fall that 2 Kings reports.
christ: Second Kings shows a people who cannot keep covenant and kings who cannot save them, and it ends with the son of David in chains, released into a foreign king's hospitality. The New Testament presents Jesus as the son of David in whom the promise that seemed nearly dead is finally kept, and Jehoiachin (called Jechoniah) stands in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1:11-12. The Elisha stories are especially important for the Gospels. Jesus himself cites Naaman the Syrian, healed when many in Israel were not, as a sign that God's mercy reaches outsiders (Luke 4:27). His feeding of the crowds, with bread left over, echoes Elisha's feeding of a hundred men with twenty loaves (2 Kings 4:42-44), and his raising of the widow's son at Nain, a village near Shunem, recalls Elisha's raising of the Shunammite's son. John the Baptist, dressed like Elijah (2 Kings 1:8; Matthew 3:4), comes in Elijah's role, and Jesus, like Elisha after Elijah, carries on a work of mercy greater than his forerunner's. These are patterns and echoes that the New Testament draws out, not predictions, and they show the kind of king and prophet Israel needed.
reading:
Second Kings is theological history in narrative prose. Its reigns are framed by regnal formulas that give the king's accession, age, length of reign, and (for Judah) his mother's name, followed by a verdict on whether he did what was right or evil in the eyes of the LORD. Northern kings are almost always said to walk in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, meaning the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. The story alternates between the two kingdoms until Israel falls, so a reader should keep track of which king is meant; confusingly, both kingdoms had kings named Jehoram (or Joram), Ahaziah, and Jehoash (or Joash) at about the same time.

Watch for prophecy and fulfillment: the narrator repeatedly notes that events happened according to the word of the LORD. The Elisha chapters are not a detour from the history but its heart, showing that God is at work in ordinary homes, among foreigners, and in a besieged city while kings fail. Some episodes are morally troubling (the bears in chapter 2, Jehu's massacres in chapters 9 and 10), and the book does not always pause to comment; a careful reader notices that later Scripture sometimes does, as when Hosea condemns the bloodshed at Jezreel (Hosea 1:4).

structure.title: Elijah's last acts and Elisha's succession
structure.summary: Elijah announces Ahaziah's death and calls down fire on the king's soldiers, then is taken up in a whirlwind, and Elisha receives his cloak and his spirit.

structure.title: The ministry of Elisha
structure.summary: Elisha's word shapes a war against Moab, provides for a widow, raises a Shunammite's son, heals Naaman, protects Israel from Aram, and announces relief for starving Samaria and Hazael's rise in Damascus.

structure.title: Jehu's purge and Joash's rescue
structure.summary: Jehu destroys the house of Ahab and the worship of Baal in Israel, while in Judah Athaliah seizes the throne and the boy Joash is hidden, crowned, and later repairs the temple.

structure.title: The last years of Israel
structure.summary: Elisha dies, the two kingdoms rise and decline, Assyria advances, and Samaria falls, followed by a long explanation of why the northern kingdom was exiled.

structure.title: Hezekiah and Manasseh
structure.summary: Hezekiah trusts the LORD and Jerusalem survives Sennacherib's siege, but his son Manasseh fills the land with idolatry and innocent blood.

structure.title: Josiah's reform and the fall of Jerusalem
structure.summary: Josiah finds the Book of the Law and purges the land, but after his death Babylon takes Jerusalem, burns the temple, and carries Judah into exile, where Jehoiachin is at last released from prison.

themes.title: The word of the LORD comes true
themes.body: Second Kings is built on prophecy and fulfillment. Elijah's word about Ahaziah, Elisha's about water, food, and war, the old prophecy against Jezebel, the warnings of the prophets against Israel and Judah: each is fulfilled, and the narrator often says so. History in this book is the arena where God's word proves itself, in mercy and in judgment.

themes.title: Idolatry and its cost
themes.body: Every king is measured by worship. The golden calves of Jeroboam, the Baal worship of Ahab's house, the high places, Manasseh's altars, and the sacrifice of children are not side issues but the reason for the exile. The book treats idolatry as covenant betrayal that corrupts a whole society, including its justice and its treatment of the weak.

themes.title: God's mercy beyond the borders
themes.body: In a book of judgment, Elisha's stories show God caring for widows, a barren woman, starving lepers, and even enemies. Naaman, the commander of a hostile army, is healed and confesses that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. The God who judges his own people is also the God of the nations.

themes.title: The lamp of David
themes.body: Twice the line of David nearly ends, when Athaliah murders the royal family and when Babylon deposes the last kings, and twice it survives, first in a hidden child and then in a released prisoner. The book never forgets God's promise to David, even when David's sons forget God.

themes.title: Reform and its limits
themes.body: Jehoash, Hezekiah, and Josiah all attempt reform, and the book honors them. Yet it also shows that reform led from the top cannot by itself change a people's heart. Josiah's is the most thorough reform in the book, and still the judgment comes, which leaves readers looking for a deeper renewal than any king could bring.

keyChapters.why: Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind, and Elisha receives his cloak and a double portion of his spirit, marking the succession of prophetic ministry.
Naaman, an Aramean commander, is healed of skin disease by washing in the Jordan and confesses the God of Israel, a story Jesus later cites.
Jehu is anointed king and destroys Joram, Ahaziah, and Jezebel, fulfilling Elijah's word against the house of Ahab.
Athaliah tries to wipe out the royal line of Judah, and the rescue and crowning of the boy Joash keeps David's line alive.
Samaria falls to Assyria, and the narrator explains at length why the northern kingdom went into exile.
Hezekiah spreads Sennacherib's threatening letter before the LORD, Isaiah answers, and Jerusalem is delivered.
The Book of the Law is found in the temple, and Josiah's response begins the greatest reform in Judah's history.
Jerusalem falls, the temple burns, and the people go into exile, yet the book ends with Jehoiachin released and fed at the king's table.

parts.body:
Second Kings is the twelfth book of the Bible. It has 25 chapters, and it covers about three centuries, from the death of King Ahaziah of Israel, about 852 BC, to 561 BC, when a captive king of Judah was let out of prison in Babylon.

The first half belongs largely to the prophet Elisha. Elijah is taken up in a whirlwind, and Elisha takes up his cloak. He provides oil for a widow, raises a mother's son, heals an enemy general of his skin disease, and sees the hills full of horses and chariots of fire. Around him the politics grind on. Moab rebels, Aram besieges Samaria, and Jehu wipes out the house of Ahab in a bloody coup. In Judah, Ahab's daughter Athaliah nearly destroys David's line, until a hidden boy is crowned in the temple.

The second half moves faster and darker. Assyria rises in the east, and Samaria falls in 722 BC. Judah lasts another century and more, under kings good and bad. Hezekiah prays, and Jerusalem is spared. His son Manasseh leads Judah into the worst idolatry in its history. Josiah finds the Book of the Law in the temple and carries out the most thorough reform any king attempted, but it cannot turn back the judgment. Babylon takes Jerusalem in 597 BC and burns it, with the temple, in 587 or 586 BC.

The book ends in exile with a quiet scene. Jehoiachin, David's descendant, is released from prison and ‘dined regularly at the king’s table for the rest of his life’ (25:29). The word of the LORD has proved true in judgment, and the promise to David is still alive.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Second Kings follows straight on from 1 Kings, where Ahab dies at Ramoth-gilead as Micaiah had said. In the Hebrew Bible the two were one book, and it completes the history that begins in Joshua and runs through Judges and Samuel. The people brought into the land lose it.

Many of the prophets whose books stand later in the Bible preached in these same reigns. Amos and Hosea spoke to the northern kingdom in the eighth century. Isaiah and Micah preached in Judah through the Assyrian crisis, and Jeremiah, Zephaniah and Habakkuk in Judah's last decades. Jonah is dated by this book to the reign of Jeroboam II (14:25). Reading 2 Kings beside them is like hearing the same years from the street and from the throne.

First and 2 Chronicles retell the period from Judah's side for the community after the exile, sometimes adding what Kings leaves out. Lamentations mourns the fall that 2 Kings reports, and Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai and Zechariah tell of a return that 2 Kings does not reach. Its first readers were Judeans in Babylon or in the ruins of Judah, asking what their history meant.

Like 1 Kings, the book does not name its author. A Jewish tradition preserved in the Babylonian Talmud names the prophet Jeremiah. The link is real in one respect: 2 Kings 24:18 to 25:30 appears almost word for word as Jeremiah 52. Most scholars today think of an editor or a school of editors who shaped older sources into the book as it stands. Those sources are named again and again at the end of a reign, the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel and of Judah, probably royal annals, now lost. The long stories of Elijah and Elisha probably came from circles of prophets who kept them.

Since Martin Noth's work in the 1940s, many scholars have read Deuteronomy through 2 Kings as one history, judged by Deuteronomy's standards: the LORD alone, worshiped at the one place he chose. Frank Moore Cross argued for a first edition under Josiah, whose reform is the book's high point, and a second in the exile. Others argue for one author working in the exile. Conservative scholars generally accept that sources were used and shaped, while stressing that the material is old and reliable.

The finished book can be no earlier than about 561 BC, the year Evil-merodach of Babylon released Jehoiachin (25:27-30). It says nothing of Cyrus's decree of 539 or 538 BC, or of any return, so most scholars date its completion to the middle of the sixth century BC, during the exile.

parts.h: Empires, dates, and what has been dug up
parts.body:
Second Kings is the story of a small people caught between empires. In the ninth century Israel's main rival was Aram, the kingdom of Damascus. Assyria was already pressing west, and from the reign of Tiglath-pileser III (745 to 727 BC), called Pul in 15:19, it turned raiding into conquest, deporting whole populations and making kingdoms into provinces. Shalmaneser V besieged Samaria, and his successor Sargon II claimed its capture. In 701 BC Sennacherib invaded Judah and took Lachish. Then Assyria collapsed: Nineveh fell in 612 BC, Josiah died at Megiddo in 609 BC confronting Pharaoh Neco, and Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC.

The kings' dates are approximate. Kingdoms counted a king's first year in different ways and sometimes had a son reigning beside his father, and scholars have proposed several reconstructions. This page follows the dates Edwin R. Thiele worked out, as the site's guide to the kings does, and says where the reckonings differ. They rarely differ by more than a few years: Samaria fell in 723 or 722 BC on Thiele's count, 722 or 721 in most histories; Jerusalem fell in 586 BC on Thiele's count, and many historians prefer 587.

From here on, outside records touch the story often. The Mesha Stele, found at Dhiban in 1868, is Moab's own account of throwing off Israel's rule (compare chapter 3). The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III shows Jehu, or his envoy, bowing and bringing tribute, an event Kings does not mention. The Tel Dan Stele, found in fragments in 1993 and 1994, is an Aramaic inscription that refers to the house of David. Sennacherib's own annals boast of Hezekiah's tribute and claim no capture of Jerusalem, and reliefs of Lachish's fall decorated his palace at Nineveh. The Siloam tunnel inscription was cut into the water tunnel usually connected with Hezekiah (20:20). The Babylonian Chronicle records the capture of Jerusalem in 597 BC, and ration tablets from Babylon name Jehoiachin, king of Judah, receiving provisions in exile.

The book has six movements. Chapters 1 and 2 tell Elijah's last acts and Elisha's succession. Chapters 3 to 8 are the ministry of Elisha. Chapters 9 to 12 tell Jehu's purge in the north and the rescue of Joash in the south. Chapters 13 to 17 tell the last years of Israel, ending with the fall of Samaria and a long explanation of why it fell. Chapters 18 to 21 belong to Hezekiah and Manasseh, and chapters 22 to 25 to Josiah's reform and the fall of Jerusalem.

Each reign is framed by a set pattern, as in 1 Kings: the year a king began, his age and, in Judah, his mother's name, how long he reigned, and a verdict on whether he did what was right or evil in the eyes of the LORD. Northern kings are almost always said to keep the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. The story moves back and forth between the two kingdoms until Israel falls, and both kingdoms had kings named Jehoram or Joram, Ahaziah, and Jehoash or Joash at about the same time, so a reader has to watch which one is meant.

Watch also for prophecy and fulfillment. Again and again the narrator notes that something happened according to the word of the LORD. The Elisha chapters are not a detour from the history. They show God at work in ordinary homes, among foreigners and in a besieged city while the kings fail.

King Ahaziah falls through a lattice and sends to ask Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether he will recover. Elijah meets his messengers with a question from the LORD: ‘Is it because there is no God in Israel’ (1:3) that they go to Ekron? Soldiers sent to seize the prophet are consumed by fire, until a third captain begs for mercy. The text presents it as the king's assault on the LORD's messenger. The New Testament refuses to make it a pattern: when two disciples wanted to call down fire from heaven on a Samaritan village, “Jesus turned and rebuked them” (Luke 9:55).

Then Elijah is taken up. Elisha will not leave him, and when Elijah asks what he can do for him, Elisha answers, “Please, let me inherit a double portion of your spirit” (2:9). ‘Suddenly a chariot of fire with horses of fire appeared and separated the two of them, and Elijah went up into heaven in a whirlwind’ (2:11). Elisha takes up the cloak and parts the Jordan with it.

At Bethel a crowd of youths jeers at him, and he curses them in the LORD's name, and bears maul forty-two of them (2:23-24). It is one of the hardest scenes in the Bible. The Hebrew words can mean young men as well as children, and the crowd's size suggests a mob from the center of the calf worship, mocking the prophet at the start of his work. Other readers, granting all of that, still find the punishment severe, and the narrator reports it without comment. The text gives no one today a warrant to harm anyone, or to curse anyone who mocks them.

Elisha's wonders reach into ordinary homes. A prophet's widow, whose creditor is coming to take her two children as slaves (4:1), is given oil enough to pay her debts. A woman of Shunem who made a room for him is given a son, and when the boy dies in her lap, Elisha raises him. Naaman, the commander of Aram's army, comes because a young girl taken captive from Israel speaks of the prophet in Samaria (5:3). He washes seven times in the Jordan and declares, “Now I know for sure that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel” (5:15). At Dothan, surrounded, Elisha prays that his servant's eyes will be opened, ‘and he saw that the hills were full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha’ (6:17).

Then famine comes to besieged Samaria, so severe that the text records mothers eating a child (6:28-29). It tells this in two verses as the curse the covenant had warned of, and these notes do not linger on it. The next day four men with leprosy find the Aramean camp deserted and say, “Today is a day of good news” (7:9). The LORD had not abandoned the city.

parts.h: Jehu, Jezebel, and a hidden king
parts.body:
Elisha sends a young prophet to anoint Jehu, an army commander, king over Israel, with a charge to destroy the house of Ahab. Jehu drives to Jezreel and kills Joram, Ahab's son, on the field that had been Naboth's. He also has Ahaziah king of Judah shot. Jezebel meets him at her window, her own servants throw her down, and the dogs leave almost nothing of her, as Elijah had said (9:36). The text tells it briefly, and these notes do the same.

In chapter 10 Jehu has Ahab's seventy sons killed, then the rest of his family and officials, forty-two relatives of the king of Judah, and the worshipers of Baal, whom he gathers into their temple by a lie. ‘Thus Jehu eradicated Baal from Israel’ (10:28). The LORD tells him, “Because you have done well in carrying out what is right in My sight”, his sons will reign to the fourth generation (10:30). The very next verse qualifies the praise: ‘Yet Jehu was not careful to follow the instruction of the LORD’ (10:31). He kept the golden calves.

About a century later the prophet Hosea named his son Jezreel, ‘for soon I will bring the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu’ (Hosea 1:4). Readers explain the tension in more than one way. Many hold that Jehu carried out a judgment on Ahab's house but went far beyond it, with cruelty and for his own ends, and that Hosea condemns the excess and the motive. Others see Jehu's purge as political, shown by his keeping the calves, so that the blood became guilt on his own house. Some critical scholars see two prophetic judgments set side by side. All agree that the chapter's verdict is mixed. Being used by God to carry out judgment does not make anyone righteous, and nothing here gives anyone a warrant to purge their enemies in God's name.

In Judah, when her son Ahaziah dies, Athaliah sets out ‘to annihilate all the royal heirs’ (11:1). His sister Jehosheba steals away the baby Joash, ‘and Joash remained hidden with his nurse in the house of the LORD for six years’ (11:3). In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada crowns him in the temple, Athaliah is put to death, and the covenant between the LORD, the king and the people is renewed. The lamp of David nearly went out, and it was kept alive in a hidden child. Joash later repairs the temple with an honest collection chest by the altar (chapter 12).

Jehu's line rules the north for nearly a century. Aram grinds Israel down, and the dying Elisha has King Jehoash strike the ground with arrows. Then the narrator stops to say why Israel survived so long: ‘But the LORD was gracious to Israel and had compassion on them, and He turned toward them because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob’ (13:23).

Under Jeroboam II Israel reaches its widest borders in generations, ‘according to the word that the LORD, the God of Israel, had spoken through His servant Jonah son of Amittai’ (14:25), not as a reward for the king, who kept the calves, but ‘For the LORD saw that the affliction of the Israelites, both slave and free, was very bitter’ (14:26). Amos, preaching in those years, saw Samaria's wealth as a sign of injustice. After Jeroboam the kingdom comes apart in about twenty-five years. Four kings are assassinated, Menahem pays tribute to Assyria, and Tiglath-pileser carries off the people of Galilee and Gilead (15:29).

In the ninth year of Hoshea, after a three-year siege, ‘the king of Assyria captured Samaria and carried away the Israelites to Assyria’ (17:6). The narrator then stops the story to explain it. Israel worshiped other gods and refused the prophets: ‘Yet through all His prophets and seers, the LORD warned Israel and Judah’ (17:13), ‘But they would not listen’ (17:14). The chapter's harshest words are aimed at Israel and then at Judah, the writer's own people, not at the foreigners. The book was written for those who had lost everything, to help them see their own history honestly.

It is not a key for reading anyone else's suffering. These chapters give no one a warrant to say that any people's suffering, then or now, is a punishment they deserved, or to point at a nation, a city or a family in trouble and pronounce God's verdict on them. They are never a reason to blame the Jewish people. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning about disaster. The chapter also tells of the peoples Assyria settled in Samaria, who worshiped the LORD alongside their own gods (17:24-41). Later Jewish writers often used it against the Samaritans, who told their own story differently, and historians think many Israelites stayed in the land. By the time of Jesus the Samaritans worshiped the LORD alone, and the New Testament treats them as people to whom the gospel belongs.

A word for anyone who has lived through a flood, a storm or another disaster. Your loss was not a judgment on you. When Jesus was asked about people killed when a tower fell, he refused that reading of a disaster: “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you are carrying this, you need people more than explanations. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page has people you can call.

Before Hezekiah came Ahaz, who ‘even sacrificed his son in the fire, according to the abominations of the nations’ (16:3). The text names the act plainly as an abomination and does not describe it. Faced with two armies, Ahaz turned to the gods of the nations and to the power of Assyria rather than the LORD, and paid Assyria with the temple's silver and gold.

His son is the opposite. ‘Hezekiah trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel. No king of Judah was like him, either before him or after him’ (18:5). He removes the high places and breaks up the bronze snake Moses made, because the people had been burning incense to it (18:4). He rebels against Assyria. When Sennacherib invades, Hezekiah first pays a heavy tribute, stripping even the gold from the temple doors, and readers differ on whether that was a lapse of faith or a king's attempt to spare a land already overrun. It does not buy safety. The Assyrian officer called the Rabshakeh stands outside the wall and asks, ‘What is the basis of this confidence of yours?’ (18:19), in Hebrew, so that the people on the wall can hear.

Hezekiah takes Sennacherib's letter into the temple, spreads it before the LORD and prays: ‘You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth’ (19:15), and ‘please save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God’ (19:19). Isaiah answers that the king of Assyria will not enter the city. That night the angel of the LORD strikes the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib goes home to Nineveh. Readers take the event in more than one way, as a direct act of God or as God acting through a sudden plague, and some question the size of the number. What is historically secure is that Sennacherib did not take Jerusalem, and his own records claim only tribute.

Then Hezekiah falls ill, prays and weeps, and is given fifteen more years. When envoys come from Babylon, he shows them everything in his treasuries, and Isaiah says it will all be carried off to Babylon one day. Hezekiah answers that the word is good, and he thinks, “Will there not at least be peace and security in my lifetime?” (20:19). The narrator gives his spoken words and his private thought, and leaves the reader to weigh them.

Hezekiah's son Manasseh reigns fifty-five years, the longest reign in Judah, and undoes everything. He rebuilds the high places, sets up altars to Baal and to the stars in the temple courts, ‘He sacrificed his own son in the fire’ and ‘consulted mediums and spiritists’ (21:6). ‘Moreover, Manasseh shed so much innocent blood that he filled Jerusalem from end to end’ (21:16). The text names child sacrifice as the shedding of innocent blood, the deepest evil a king could do, and these notes do not describe it.

A word for anyone who was not protected by a parent, or was handed over to harm by someone who should have kept them safe. This story does not call that right. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Through the prophets the LORD says that Jerusalem will be judged as Samaria was. Kings never mentions the repentance that 2 Chronicles 33 reports of Manasseh. Some historians think Chronicles preserves a real episode that Kings left out because it did not change the outcome, and others think the Chronicler shaped the story to teach that God answers repentance in every generation.

Then comes Josiah, made king at eight after his father Amon is murdered. In his eighteenth year, during repairs to the temple, the high priest Hilkiah says, “I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD!” (22:8). When it is read, the king tears his clothes. The prophetess Huldah confirms that disaster will come on Jerusalem, but because Josiah's heart was tender, ‘Your eyes will not see all the calamity that I will bring on this place’ (22:20). Josiah reads the book to all the people, ‘all the people small and great’ (23:2), and makes a covenant before the LORD. He purges the temple and the land, from Jerusalem to the altar at Bethel, and keeps a Passover like none since the judges.

‘Neither before nor after Josiah was there any king like him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his strength, according to all the Law of Moses’ (23:25). And yet the next verse begins, ‘Nevertheless’ (23:26). Reform led from the top could not by itself turn a people's heart. Josiah is killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Neco (23:29), and his sons rule under Egypt and then Babylon.

parts.h: The fall of Jerusalem, and a king at the table
parts.body:
Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon makes Jehoiakim his vassal, and Jehoiakim rebels. His son Jehoiachin reigns three months and surrenders in 597 BC. Nebuchadnezzar carries off the king, the royal family, the leaders, the soldiers and the craftsmen, strips the temple's gold, and sets up Jehoiachin's uncle Zedekiah as king. The narrator says it happened because of Manasseh's sins and the innocent blood he shed, ‘and the LORD was unwilling to forgive’ (24:4). That refusal concerns the verdict on Jerusalem as a city and a kingdom. It does not set a limit on God's mercy toward anyone who turns to him; Jeremiah, in these same years, called people to repent and promised a new covenant.

Zedekiah rebels too. Babylon besieges Jerusalem until famine breaks the city. Zedekiah flees by night and is caught near Jericho. His sons are killed in front of him, and he is blinded and taken to Babylon (25:7). A month later Nebuzaradan ‘burned down the house of the LORD, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem’ (25:9) and broke down the walls. The people are carried into exile, and only the poorest are left. The text tells the destruction in a few plain lines and does not linger over it.

Kings gives its own answer to why. King and people broke the covenant again and again, despite generations of warning. Lamentations grieves the same fall without pretending to understand everything, and Psalm 89 cries out that God seems to have renounced his covenant with David. Both are in the Bible. As with the fall of Samaria, this is Judah's own Scripture judging Judah's own kings. It gives no one a warrant to say that any people's suffering, then or now, is a punishment they deserved, and it is never a reason to blame the Jewish people.

The last scene comes thirty-seven years into the exile. The new king of Babylon releases Jehoiachin from prison, speaks kindly to him, sets his throne above the other captive kings, ‘So Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes, and he dined regularly at the king’s table for the rest of his life’ (25:29). The writer does not explain why he ends there. Readers have long seen in it a small light: David's line had not been cut off, and the story was not over.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads 2 Kings
parts.body:
Jesus himself pointed to Elisha. At Nazareth he reminded his hometown, ‘there were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet. Yet not one of them was cleansed’ (Luke 4:27), except Naaman the Syrian. God's mercy had reached an enemy general, and Jesus would not let his hearers forget it.

Elijah, taken up in 2 Kings 2, stands behind John the Baptist. The angel told Zechariah that his son would go before the Lord ‘in the spirit and power of Elijah’ (Luke 1:17). The king's men had described Elijah as ‘a hairy man’ with ‘a leather belt around his waist’ (1:8), and Matthew says that John ‘wore a garment of camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist’ (Matthew 3:4). When two disciples wanted to call down fire as Elijah had, Jesus rebuked them (Luke 9:54-55).

Matthew's family tree of Jesus runs through the kings of this book: ‘Uzziah was the father of Jotham, Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah’, and on through Manasseh, Amon and Josiah to ‘Jeconiah and his brothers at the time of the exile to Babylon’ (Matthew 1:9-11). Jeconiah is Jehoiachin, the king released at the end of the book. The promise to David passed through faithful hands and through some of the worst kings in the Bible, and through the exile itself.

The New Testament draws those lines and no others from this book. It does not make every prophet or king in 2 Kings a picture of Christ. And nothing in 2 Kings, or in the New Testament's use of it, gives anyone reason to blame or look down on the Jewish people. This is Israel's own Scripture, telling the truth about Israel's own kings and grieving Israel's own losses.

Read it as history with a question. Watch the verdict on each reign, and watch the prophets. A word spoken in one chapter comes true in another, sometimes centuries later, as when Josiah burns bones on the altar at Bethel that a man of God had cried out against in 1 Kings 13. Watch the lamp kept for David ‘for the sake of His servant David’ (8:19), through a hidden child and a released prisoner.

Do not read prosperity as proof of God's approval, or disaster as proof of anyone's guilt. Jeroboam II prospered and did evil; Josiah was the best of kings and died in battle. Do not read the fire on the soldiers, the bears, Jehu's purge or Josiah's killing of the priests of the high places as a pattern for today. The New Testament gives the church no sword in matters of worship, and these chapters give no one a warrant for violence. And do not be surprised when the reforming kings fall short. The book honors Jehoash, Hezekiah and Josiah, and still shows that reform from the top cannot by itself change a people's heart.

Two places are worth reading slowly: Hezekiah's prayer with the enemy's letter spread before the LORD (chapter 19), and the last four verses, where a captive king changes out of his prison clothes. The story runs on in the books that come after it: in Lamentations' grief, in the prophets of the exile, and in Ezra and Nehemiah, where the people come home.

hard.line: Fire on two captains and their fifty men, who came on their king's orders.
Elisha curses a jeering crowd at Bethel, and two bears maul forty-two of them.
Mesha sacrifices his son on the wall, and great fury falls on Israel: whose fury?
A creditor coming to take a widow's two children as slaves.
A mother's only son dies in her lap, and she goes to the prophet.
Naaman asks pardon in advance for bowing in the temple of Rimmon, and Elisha says, Go in peace.
Gehazi's greed, and Naaman's disease on him and his descendants.
Famine in besieged Samaria, and a king who blames God.
The officer who scoffed is trampled to death in the gate.
Did Elisha tell Hazael to lie to the king, or encourage him to murder?
Jehu kills Joram on Naboth's land and has Ahaziah of Judah shot.
Jezebel thrown from a window, as Elijah had said.
Ahab's seventy sons killed at Jehu's command.
God praises Jehu's purge, and Hosea later condemns the blood of Jezreel.
Athaliah sets out to destroy the royal family, and a baby is hidden.
Kings speaks well of Joash, and Chronicles tells of his turning and a prophet stoned.
Elisha angry at a king who struck the ground three times.
A dead man revived at the touch of Elisha's bones.
Jeroboam II did evil, and Israel prospered under him.
Menahem's atrocity at Tiphsah, reported without comment.
Ahaz sacrifices his son in the fire.
The fall of Samaria explained as judgment.
The settlers in Samaria, and the Samaritans' own story.
Hezekiah, who trusted the LORD, pays tribute and strips the temple doors.
The Assyrian camp struck in one night.
Hezekiah hears of exile to come and thinks of peace in his own lifetime.
Manasseh's child sacrifice and the innocent blood that filled Jerusalem.
Huldah promised Josiah a peaceful grave, and he died in battle.
Josiah kills the priests of the high places on their altars.
‘The LORD was unwilling to forgive’: what that means.
Zedekiah's sons killed before his eyes.
If God chose Jerusalem, how could he let the city and the temple burn?

words.line: A prophet, someone sent with God's word. Elisha is called this again and again, and the woman of Shunem calls him a holy man of God (4:9).
Groups of prophets who lived and worked together around a senior prophet such as Elijah or Elisha (2:3; 4:38).
In Hebrew ruach: spirit, wind or breath. Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's (2:9), the share of the firstborn heir.
Elisha's cry as Elijah is taken (2:12), and the king's cry over the dying Elisha (13:14): the prophet was Israel's real defense.
In Hebrew tsara'at, a range of skin diseases, not only what is called leprosy today. Naaman had it (5:1), and so did four men at Samaria's gate (7:3).
A picture of a family line kept alive. The LORD had promised to maintain a lamp for David (8:19).
The golden calves at Bethel and Dan, which every northern king kept, even Jehu (10:29).
In Hebrew bamah, local hilltop shrines. Even good kings left them, until Hezekiah removed them (18:4).
A Canaanite goddess, and the wooden pole that stood for her. Manasseh set up a carved Asherah pole in the temple (21:7).
The Hebrew phrase behind the BSB's sacrificed in the fire (16:3; 21:6). Most scholars read it as child sacrifice, which the prophets call innocent blood.
An Assyrian title, a chief officer, not a name. He mocked Hezekiah's trust outside Jerusalem's wall (18:17-35).
The bronze snake Moses made, which the people had turned into an idol. Hezekiah broke it up (18:4).
The scroll found in the temple in Josiah's eighteenth year (22:8), called the Book of the Covenant when he reads it to the people (23:2). Many scholars connect it with Deuteronomy.
Those who are left after judgment. Isaiah promised that a remnant would go out from Jerusalem (19:30-31).
Being carried off from the land. Israel went to Assyria (17:6), and Judah to Babylon (24:14-16; 25:21).

timeline.what: Ahaziah of Israel dies after his fall, as Elijah had said (1:17), and his brother Joram reigns.
Joram reigns in Israel, and Elisha's ministry fills chapters 3 to 8. Moab rebels (chapter 3), and Mesha tells his side on a stone found at Dhiban in 1868.
Jehu kills Joram and Ahaziah and takes Israel's throne (chapter 9). Albright's reckoning gives 842. The same year Jehu, or his envoy, brings tribute to Shalmaneser III, shown on the Black Obelisk.
Athaliah rules Judah, until the priest Jehoiada crowns Joash in the temple (chapter 11).
Jehoash reigns in Israel. Elisha dies in his reign, after the arrows of victory (13:14-20).
Jeroboam II restores Israel's borders, as Jonah had said (14:25). Amos and Hosea preach in the north.
Tiglath-pileser III, called Pul (15:19), rules Assyria and begins deporting conquered peoples. Menahem pays him tribute.
Aram and Israel attack Judah; Ahaz appeals to Assyria, which takes Damascus and Galilee (15:29; 16:5-9).
Samaria falls after a three-year siege (17:5-6). Most histories give 722 or 721. Sargon II claimed the capture and the deportation.
Hezekiah reigns in Judah, removes the high places and rebels against Assyria (chapter 18). Galil's reckoning gives 726 to 697.
Sennacherib invades Judah, takes Lachish and besieges Jerusalem, but does not take it (chapters 18 and 19).
Manasseh reigns fifty-five years, at first beside his father (21:1).
In Josiah's eighteenth year the Book of the Law is found in the temple (22:3-8).
Nineveh, Assyria's capital, falls to the Babylonians and Medes.
Josiah is killed at Megiddo confronting Pharaoh Neco (23:29).
Nebuchadnezzar defeats Egypt at Carchemish, and Judah becomes Babylon's vassal (24:1).
Jerusalem surrenders; Jehoiachin and thousands are carried to Babylon (24:10-16). The Babylonian Chronicle records it.
Jerusalem and the temple are burned (25:8-10). Many historians prefer 587.
Evil-merodach releases Jehoiachin from prison (25:27-30). The finished book of Kings can be no earlier.

map.title: Israel and Judah in the days of Elisha and the last kings

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: David's city. Sennacherib's officers mocked Hezekiah outside its wall (18:17-35), the LORD defended it (19:34), and Babylon burned it (25:8-10).

places.name: Bethel
places.line: Elijah and Elisha passed through it (2:2-3), youths jeered at Elisha on the road up (2:23), and Josiah tore down its altar (23:15).

places.name: Jericho
places.line: Elisha healed its spring (2:19-22). Zedekiah was overtaken in its plains as he fled (25:5).

places.name: The Jordan
places.line: Elijah and then Elisha parted it with the cloak (2:8, 14), and Naaman washed in it seven times (5:14).

places.name: Samaria
places.line: The northern hill country, named after Israel's capital, which Aram besieged (6:24) and Assyria took after three years (17:5-6). The book also uses the name for the region (17:24). Drawn roughly; the city is not marked.

places.name: Dothan
places.line: Where the Arameans surrounded Elisha, and his servant saw the hills full of horses and chariots of fire (6:13-17).

places.name: Gilead
places.line: The land east of the Jordan. Jehu was anointed at Ramoth-gilead (9:1-6), Hazael took it (10:32-33), and Assyria carried off its people (15:29). Drawn roughly.

places.name: Damascus
places.line: Capital of Aram, Naaman's home (5:12). Elisha went there and wept before Hazael (8:7-15), and Assyria took it (16:9).

places.name: Beersheba
places.line: The southern edge of Judah. Joash's mother came from here (12:1), and Josiah defiled the high places ‘from Geba to Beersheba’ (23:8).

teaching.mapNote: Only nine places are drawn, each placed elsewhere on this site; Samaria and Gilead roughly, as regions. Gilgal, Shunem, Jezreel, Megiddo, Lachish, Ekron, Moab and Edom are left off, because where they lay is debated or is not placed in this site's records, and so are Assyria, Babylon and Egypt. No borders are drawn. The map makes no claim about any border today.
